'''''Lepidium heterophyllum''''' ('''Smith's cress''' or '''Smith's pepperwort''') is a species of flowering plant in the [[Brassicaceae|mustard family]] which is native to parts of western [[Europe]], growing in shingle banks, wasteland or cultivated fields.

==Description==
''Lepidium heterophyllum'' is similar in form to native ''[[Lepidium campestre]]'' and especially at the early seedling stage, both have been misidentified in [[Belgium]].<ref name="belgium">{{cite web|title=Lepidium heterophyllum|url=http://alienplantsbelgium.be/content/lepidium-heterophyllum|date=19 July 2012|publisher=alienplantsbelgium.be|access-date=26 November 2017}}</ref>

It is a [[perennial]],<ref name="efloras">{{cite web|title=FNA Vol. 7 Page 571, 578, 582, 583|url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=250095029|publisher=efloras.org|access-date=26 November 2017}}</ref> which can grow between {{convert|10|-|90|cm|abbr=on}} tall.<ref name=Readers>{{cite book |year=1981 |title=Reader's Digest Field Guide to the Wild Flowers of Britain |page=51 |publisher=[[Reader's Digest]] |isbn=978-0-276-00217-5}}</ref> The hirsute (or hairy) stems,<ref name="efloras"/> are often branched from the base,<ref name=Readers/><ref name="efloras"/><ref name=Harrap>Simon Harrap {{google books|rwRpBAAAQBAJ|Harrap's Wild Flowers (2013)|page=130}}</ref> It has grey-green foliage,<ref name=Harrap/> that has narrowly triangular,<ref name=Readers/><ref name=Harrap/> variably toothed,<ref name=Harrap/> stem leaves which cling to the stem with long pointed [[Auricle (botany)|auricles]].<ref name=Harrap/><ref name="efloras"/> The stem leaves can grow up to 50 mm long.<ref name=Harrap/> The basal leaves are different, they have long stalks and are strap-shape,<ref name=Harrap/> or oblong-elliptic.<ref name="efloras"/> They can often have 1-3 pairs of small but broad sided lobes, they quickly fade at blooming time but can re-grow as the plant goes to seed.<ref name=Harrap/> It blooms between May and August,<ref name=Readers/> or between May and September, in the UK,<ref name=Harrap/> and between May and July in the US.<ref name="efloras"/> The very small flowers ({{convert|2|-|3.6|mm|abbr=on}} long,<ref name=Harrap/>) are on short stalks at right angles to the stem, the plant can have several crowded, parallel-sided flower spikes.<ref name=Harrap/> The white spatulate (spoon-shaped) petals,<ref name="efloras"/> are as long as the oblong sepals.<ref name=Readers/> and 6 styles, which have a notch.<ref name=Harrap/><ref name="efloras"/> The flower also has [[stamens]] with violet anthers.<ref name=Readers/> After it has flowered, it produces a fruit capsule, which is oval and smooth, with a distinctive beak at the top.<ref name=Readers/> They are ({{convert|4.5|-|8.6|mm|abbr=on}} long,<ref name=Harrap/> and inside are ovoid dark brown seeds.<ref name="efloras"/>

==Phytochemistry==
It was found after a [[phylogenetic]] analysis of the [[DNA]] of many species of 'Lepidium', that ''Lepidium heterophyllum'', ''[[Lepidium hirtum]]'', ''Lepidium campestre'', and ''[[Lepidium perfoliatum]]'' formed a [[monophyletic]] group.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Lee|first1=Ji-Young|last2=Mummenhoff|first2=Klaus|last3=Bowman|first3=John L.|title=Allopolyploidization and evolution of species with reduced floral structures in Lepidium L. (Brassicaceae)|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America|date=24 December 2002|volume=99|issue=26|pages=16835–16840|doi=10.1073/pnas.242415399|pmc=139230|pmid=12481035|bibcode=2002PNAS...9916835L|doi-access=free}}</ref>

It has been used in experiments growing in soils high in [[copper]] content, to determine if the plant could be used to help clean contaminated soils.
<ref name="soil">Irena Twardowska, Herbert E. Allen and Max M. Häggblom (Editors) {{google books|0v6Tu4kI7s8C|Soil and Water Pollution Monitoring, Protection and Remediation|page=193}}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
It was published and described by [[George Bentham]] in 'Cat. Pl. Pyrénées' on page 95 in 1826.<ref name="Plantlist"/><ref name="efloras"/><ref name="Ipni">{{cite web|title=Brassicaceae Lepidium heterophyllum Benth.|url=http://www.ipni.org/ipni/idPlantNameSearch.do?id=286210-1|publisher=ipni.org|access-date=26 November 2017}}</ref>

It has one known [[subspecies]]; ''Lepidium heterophyllum'' subsp. ''rifanum'' (Emb. & Maire) J.M.Monts.<ref name="Plantlist"/>

The [[Botanical name#Binary name|specific epithet]] ''heterophyllum'', refers to the Greek for 'different leaves'.<ref>{{cite web|title=Myriophyllum heterophyllum Michx.|url=http://swbiodiversity.org/seinet/taxa/index.php?taxon=18447|publisher=swbiodiversity.org|access-date=27 November 2017}}</ref>

It has a few common names including 'Smith's cress' and 'Smith's pepperwort',<ref name="rhs">{{cite web|title=Lepidium heterophyllum|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/9945|publisher=rhs.org.uk|access-date=26 November 2017}}</ref> this is due to the plant once being named ''Lepidium smithii'', by [[Sir William Hooker]], in honour of the botanist, [[Sir James Edward Smith]].<ref name=Readers/> This name is now regarded as a synonym.<ref name="Plantlist"/>
It is also known in the US, as 'purple antherfield pepperwort'<ref>Tim Johnson {{google books|vxAaBv8fW00C|CRC Ethnobotany Desk Reference|page=464}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=purpleanther field pepperweed|url=https://www.invasiveplantatlas.org/subject.html?sub=45166|publisher=invasiveplantatlas.org|access-date=29 November 2017}}</ref><ref>Joseph M. DiTomaso and Evelyn A. Healy {{google books|REZnaLndgoAC|Weeds of California and Other Western States, Volume 1 (2007)|page=1786}}</ref> The pepperwort name came from plant looking like a 'pepperwort' (''Lepidium campestre'' or other Lepidium species).<ref name=Readers/>

==Distribution and habitat==
[[File:Lepidium heterophyllum Habitus 2010-3-21 SierraMadrona.jpg|thumb|Plant seen in [[Sierra Madrona]], Spain]]
''Lepidium heterophyllum'' is [[native plant|native]] to [[temperate]] areas of western Europe.<ref name="rhs"/><ref name="Ipni"/><ref name="Grin">{{cite web|title=Taxon: Lepidium heterophyllum Benth.|url=https://npgsweb.ars-grin.gov/gringlobal/taxonomydetail.aspx?id=316723|publisher=npgsweb.ars-grin.gov|access-date=28 November 2017}}</ref>

===Range===
It is found in Europe within [[Denmark]], [[France]], [[Germany]], [[Ireland]], the [[Netherlands]], [[Portugal]], [[Spain]] and the [[United Kingdom]].<ref name="Grin"/>

It is also widely [[naturalisation (biology)|naturalised]] in other parts of Europe such as Belgium, the [[Czech Republic]], [[Finland]], [[Norway]] and [[Sweden]]. As well as [[Canada]], [[Chile]] and the [[United States]].<ref name="Grin"/> It has been recorded as found in [[British Columbia]], [[Newfoundland and Labrador]], [[California]], [[Colorado]], [[Maine]], [[Massachusetts]], [[New York (state)]], [[Oregon]], [[Pennsylvania]] and [[Washington (U.S. state)|Washington (state)]].<ref name="efloras"/> The records from Maine and Massachusetts are based on old plant collections, and it is not fully known if the plant has become established as part of the weedy flora of those states.<ref name="efloras"/> In Belgium, it was first recorded in fallow fields between 1881 and 1884 in [[Egenhoven]], and then in 1886 near [[Bouillon, Belgium|Bouillon]]. Later, it was observed in [[Stokt]] (in the province of [[Limburg (Netherlands)|Limburg]], Netherlands), in the 19th century. Recently, in 2004 and 2005, it was recorded on gravelly riverbanks of [[River Maas]] (which rises in France and flowing through Belgium and the Netherlands to the North Sea).<ref name="brc"/>

===Habitat===
It is found growing in [[Soil pH|acidic soils]],<ref name="iucn status 12 November 2021" /><ref name="brc">{{cite web|title=Lepidium heterophyllum|url=https://www.brc.ac.uk/plantatlas/plant/lepidium-heterophyllum|publisher=brc.ac.uk ([[Biological Records Centre]])|access-date=26 November 2017}}</ref> on hillsides,<ref name="efloras"/> in [[Shingle beach|shingle]], railway ballast and embankments, and, occasionally, in [[Arable land|arable fields]].<ref name="iucn status 12 November 2021" /><ref name=Harrap/><ref name="brc"/>

It is normally found at altitudes of {{convert|0|–|425|m|ft|abbr=on}} above sea level.<ref name="iucn status 12 November 2021" /><ref name=Harrap/><ref name="brc"/><!-- also<ref name="efloras">-->

==Conservation==
Populations of ''Lepidium heterophyllum'' currently are stable, but it seems to be decreasing in S.E. England.<ref name="brc"/>
